terms.comment: Levi and Bini’s phrase for the Italian affettare, to cut into slices (p. 2). Frusta are pieces or bits, classically of food (in frusta secant, Verg. A. 1.212, Lewis & Short); dissecāre, to cut in pieces, is post-Augustan and frequent in the elder Pliny (Lewis & Short).
Our phrase on segmentum, which is the slice of Traupman (pp. 73, 380) and Morgan–Owens (s.v. slice) and “a piece cut off, a slice” in Lewis & Short; frusta are pieces of any shape.

phrases.latin: pars in frusta secant veribusque trementia fīgunt
phrases.english: some cut the meat into pieces and fix it, still quivering, on spits

sources: Lewis & Short: disseco · Lewis & Short: frustum · Lewis & Short: segmentum
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 2, s.v. affettare.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 73, 380.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. slice.
